endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Deploying AI in clinical environments creates a dynamic attack surface that must be continuously evaluated.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Also note whether data and model security are routinely monitored, and whether the timescales and frequency of security checks have been defined and adequately justified.

endorsements.title: Action Guide: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
endorsements.issuer: National Association of Community Health Centers
endorsements.quote: AI implementation must comply with HIPAA (Health Insurance and Portability and Accountability Act), obtain appropriate patient consent, and follow rigorous security practices such as encryption, access controls, and regular audits.

endorsements.title: Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare (RUAIH) guidance
endorsements.issuer: The Joint Commission and Coalition for Health AI
endorsements.quote: Regular Security Assessments: Conduct regular security assessments and vulnerability scans to identify and address potential security risks and mitigate known vulnerabilities and risks.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Apply established security measures to: Assess likelihood and magnitude of vulnerabilities and threats such as backdoors, compromised dependencies, data breaches, eavesdropping, man-in-the-middle attacks, reverse engineering, autonomous agents, model theft or exposure of model weights, AI inference, bypass, extraction, and other baseline security concerns.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
Ethical Considerations of Using ChatGPT in Health Care
endorsements.quote: To mitigate privacy risks, health care organizations should implement robust security measures, including encryption, access controls, and regular vulnerability assessments [ 10 ].

endorsements.title: Charting the future of patient care: A strategic leadership guide to harnessing the potential of artificial intelligence
endorsements.quote: Healthcare organizations are obligated to conduct regular audits and compliance checks to ensure adherence to data protection regulations.

endorsements.title: Chatbots in medicine: certification process and applied use case
endorsements.quote: Regular audits and stress tests should be conducted to ensure compliance with security standards.

endorsements.title: Computational Nuclear Oncology Toward Precision Radiopharmaceutical Therapies: Ethical, Regulatory, and Socioeconomic Dimensions of Theranostic Digital Twins
endorsements.issuer: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
endorsements.quote: Regular security assessments and audits are integral to promptly identifying and addressing vulnerabilities.

endorsements.title: Ethical framework for responsible foundational models in medical imaging
endorsements.quote: Regular security audits serve as critical checkpoints, identifying potential vulnerabilities and enabling proactive implementation of protective measures against emerging threats.

endorsements.title: Collaborative framework on responsible AI in LLM-driven CDSS for precision oncology leveraging real-world patient data
endorsements.quote: For the protection of patient data and patient well-being robust infrastructure is a key principle of applying generative AI to real-world patient data, necessitating cybersecurity safeguards and regular internal and external audits.

endorsements.title: Legal, ethical, and policy challenges of artificial intelligence translation tools in healthcare
endorsements.quote: To maintain high standards of data protection, healthcare institutions should conduct regular audits of the AI tools they use [ 62 ].

evidence.title: Caging the Agents: A Zero Trust Security Architecture for Autonomous AI in Healthcare
evidence.outcome: Vulnerabilities found by automated security audit agent during 90-day deployment
evidence.effect: Automated security audit agent discovered four HIGH severity findings over 90 days, all remediated; fleet hardened across three VM image generations.
evidence.quote: We report results from 90 days of deployment including four HIGH severity findings discovered and remediated by an automated security audit agent, progressive fleet hardening across three VM image generations, and defense coverage mapped to all eleven attack patterns from recent literature.

commentary.bottom_line: One uncontrolled 90-day study of nine autonomous AI agents found that an automated security audit agent surfaced four high-severity vulnerabilities, all of which were remediated, which suggests recurring scanning can find real flaws. No study has tested a documented vulnerability management plan for clinical AI systems or measured effects on breaches or patient harm.

perspectives.view: The only test is a pre-post study without a comparator, involving nine AI agents in an unreported setting. It counts findings and remediations but does not measure breaches prevented. The design is weak, the population is indirect to clinical AI, the sample is small, and no second study exists to check consistency. Certainty is very low.

Four high-severity findings in 90 days on nine agents suggest that deployed AI systems carry exploitable flaws that routine auditing can surface before an attacker does. The study does not link these findings to any clinical data exposure or patient harm, so the size of the safety benefit in health care remains unknown.

The study hardened the fleet across three virtual machine image generations, which indicates that audit findings fed back into the build process. The study did not report how the audit agent fit into clinical workflows, how much staff time remediation took, or how often scans produced false alarms.

Twelve sources endorse the practice, including the FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software, NIST AI 600-1, and CHAI, and three rate it as a requirement. The endorsements rest on established cybersecurity practice and HIPAA security expectations rather than on trials in clinical AI, and CHAI asks organizations to define and justify scan frequency.

The tested approach used an automated audit agent, which may lower the staffing needed for recurring scans. The study reported no costs, and it did not describe the effort required for penetration testing or external audits, so health systems have no evidence to budget from beyond general security program experience.

commentary.research_gap: Health systems need controlled or comparative studies of vulnerability management programs for deployed clinical AI, including large language model and device software, that measure breaches, data exposure, time to remediation, false alarm burden, and cost, and that compare scan frequencies and automated versus human testing.
commentary.underserved_note: The single study did not report its setting or any patient population, and it did not include Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net organizations often have smaller security staffs and budgets, so the evidence cannot show whether the practice is feasible or effective where breach risk may fall on patients with the fewest resources to respond.
